problems.description: Replaces the seed's modular Blueprint-based structure (auth_bp, items_bp) with a flat single-module Flask app, collapsing separation of concerns that the previous tier-2 structure established.
Removes the token auth layer (users/tokens tables, require_auth decorator) entirely, leaving all /tasks routes unauthenticated; intentional for greenfield but drops prior security scaffolding.

10 convention violations across new files: classes not PascalCase (app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py, tasks.py) and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (app.py, conftest.py, repositories.py), matching the 0.70 convention score.
celery_config.py introduces functions not in snake_case, inconsistent with the snake_case function convention used in the rest of the codebase.
Database filename switched to 'tasks.db' and the flat single-file layout moves away from the modular multi-file pattern the seed was designed to demonstrate.

strengths: Adds +3 files (repositories.py, tasks.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py), indicating attempted layering beyond a monolith.
Uses parameterized queries for all SQL, avoiding injection issues despite removing the auth layer.
Compact greenfield rewrite netting -202 lines in app.py with clear 400/201 error handling.
commit_reviews.summary: Greenfield rewrite that trades the seed's modular Blueprint architecture for a flat single-module app and logs a 0.70 convention score, making it net worse on structure while adding some layering.

problems.description: app.config["SECRET_KEY"] falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-change-me' value; any deployment that forgets the env var ships with a known signing key for all JWTs.

owner_id is defined in the CREATE TABLE tasks schema and then re-added via ALTER TABLE inside init_db; the try/except OperationalError swallowing makes the migration path implicit and hard to reason about.

Mechanical score 0.70 but the 10 listed violations are mostly naming issues (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants) in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) or files where this commit adds no classes/constants — likely pre-existing, not introduced here. Flagged discrepancy.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated on Python 3.12; new code should prefer datetime.now(timezone.utc).
conftest auth_headers fixture inlines raw JSON string literals while test_app.py uses json.dumps — inconsistent style between fixture and tests.
register does not return a token, forcing a second round-trip to login; minor API ergonomics gap, not a correctness issue.

strengths: Passwords hashed via werkzeug generate_password_hash, never returned in responses (register excludes password field)
Every task route enforces ownership with AND owner_id = ?, closing IDOR data-exposure risk on get/update/list
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON enables FK enforcement for the new users/tasks relationship
Consistent use of existing patterns: get_db(), jsonify, silent=True request parsing, route decorators
Solid test coverage for the new auth flow via fixtures; sonar shows smells -3 and no new bugs/duplication
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped, properly-tested auth + per-user ownership feature that follows the app's existing Flask/sqlite patterns and improves security posture, with only minor debt from a hardcoded secret fallback, a redundant schema migration, and a deprecated utcnow call — while the 0.70 convention score mostly reflects pre-existing naming violations in files outside this diff.

problems.description: Measured convention score 0.70 with 10 violations across app.py, celery_config.py, conftest.py, repositories.py, and tasks.py (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE naming flagged). Some are false positives for test classes/fixtures, but the flagged module-level and config naming issues are real.
email column is added both in the users CREATE TABLE and via a separate ALTER TABLE in init_db(), duplicating schema handling for fresh databases.

conftest.py autouse fixture _mock_notification_task and per-test monkeypatch.setattr both patch the same tasks.send_notification_email.delay attribute; their overlapping teardown order makes the autouse fixture's guard redundant and fragile.
send_notification_email is a print() stub rather than a real email delivery, so the async plumbing is untested end-to-end.
Synthetic fallback emails (f"user{id}@example.com") and unvalidated email input mean notifications can be silently routed to wrong addresses.
Cognitive complexity of update_task grew by +17 per SonarQube, concentrating notification logic inside the route handler instead of a service layer.

strengths: Async email notification correctly decoupled via Celery task queue instead of blocking the request path
Transition detection (old_status != 'completed' and status == 'completed') avoids duplicate notifications on re-submission
Comprehensive test coverage for trigger, non-trigger, idempotency, and nonexistent-task cases
Migration approach (try/except ALTER TABLE) matches the existing owner_id pattern in the codebase
Graceful handling of missing email with fallback values
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested async notification feature that fits the existing Flask/sqlite architecture and migration conventions, slightly marred by naming violations (0.70), duplicated schema handling, and an email-stub that adds minor technical debt.

problems.description: flask_limiter is imported and used but no requirements.txt update appears in the diff, so the new dependency is undeclared and installs will fail.
Limiter storage_uri defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0, silently coupling production to a running Redis at import time; a missing/misconfigured RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URL breaks app startup.

list_tasks response contract changed from a bare JSON array to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope, a breaking API change with no migration/versioning; tests were updated but existing clients would break.
Rate-limit key_func decodes the JWT on every request (including unauthenticated /auth calls where it catches and falls back to IP), adding per-request decode overhead to the hot path.
New module-level `limiter` is lowercase; SonarQube flags module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE. It matches the existing `app`/`task_repo` instance-naming style, but the checker still counts it.
A single uniform limit (100 per minute) is applied to all endpoints including authenticated ones; no differentiated tiers for auth vs. task routes.

strengths: Rate limiting applied as a decorator mirrors the existing token_required pattern and is config-driven via env vars.
Cursor (keyset) pagination implemented in the repository layer via find_paginated_by_owner, respecting the existing repository abstraction.
Comprehensive pagination tests added and conftest.py isolates rate-limit storage (memory://) so tests need no Redis.
429 error handler returns a proper JSON body with Retry-After header; key_func cleanly scopes limits per-user when a token is present.
SonarQube confirms zero new bugs, fewer smells (-2), and no code duplication.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-patterned cross-cutting session that cleanly adds rate limiting and cursor pagination with strong tests, but ships an undeclared dependency, a hardcoded Redis storage default, and a breaking list_tasks contract.

compounding_issues: Schema evolution via guarded ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN (owner_id, email) instead of a migration system; later sessions had to bolt columns onto the Session 1 tasks table
Celery 'email notification' is a print() mock (tasks.py), so the S3 integration layer is non-functional beyond logging, limiting what S5 could build on
owner_id was added to tasks in S2 but users table came with it, yet auth gating only fully hardened in S5 — auth was spread across multiple sessions
Inline get_db()/sqlite connection handling persisted through S1-S3, so the S4 repository extraction required touching every route at once
key_decisions: Choosing Flask + SQLite with a single tasks table and inline connection factory in S1, which fixed the persistence approach for the whole story
Introducing owner-scoped access and user auth (token_required, register/login) in S2 via ALTER TABLE migrations
Integrating Celery + Redis broker for async notification delivery in S3 (celery_config.py, tasks.py)
Extracting a BaseRepository/TaskRepository abstraction in S4 to slim app.py and isolate DB access
Adding cross-cutting rate limiting and email column in S5, closing the auth/security loop
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and deliberately across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a minimal but clean single-file CRUD API; Session 2 layered in user auth and per-owner data scoping with pragmatic ALTER migrations; Session 3 added a Celery async integration seam; Session 4 was a genuine refactor that extracted a repository layer and cut app.py by ~45%; Session 5 added rate limiting and final hardening. The test suite grew from 180 to 325 lines and ended at 46 passing tests, so each session built on and validated the prior state rather than degrading it.
story_review.summary: A well-orchestrated, textbook incremental build where each session added a distinct architectural layer on top of the last, ending with a passing, feature-complete API — the only real friction points being late-arriving schema migrations and a non-functional email mock.
